Interpreting the scoranet diagnostic figures

Source: DIAGNOSTICS.md

This guide explains what each diagnostic figure shows, what a healthy result looks like, and which settings to change when it doesn’t look healthy. All figures come from run_network_diagnostics(), or from the individual functions it calls.

dx <- run_network_diagnostics(net_list, de_list, go_list, outdir = "results/diagnostics/")

Contents

  1. Recommended order
  2. Comparison overview
  3. Overlap threshold diagnostic
  4. Leiden resolution sweep
  5. Driver genes per cluster
  6. The network plots themselves
  7. Quick reference

Recommended order

The settings depend on each other, so check them in this order:

  1. Overview. Which cell types have enough signal to bother with?
  2. Overlap threshold. It decides which terms are in the network at all.
  3. Leiden resolution. It decides how the remaining terms are grouped. Choose it after the threshold, because changing the threshold changes the network the resolution acts on.
  4. Driver genes. Read these last, to interpret the clusters you settled on.

1. Comparison overview

plot_comparison_overview(de_list, go_list, net_list)

What it shows. For each cell type, three panels of bar counts:

Panel Counts
DEGs Genes passing padj_thresh and logfc_thresh, split into up in the numerator and up in the denominator
Enriched GO terms Significant terms from run_go_ora(); split by direction if ORA was run with split_direction = TRUE, otherwise one grey “Combined” bar
Network clusters Leiden clusters in each cell type’s network, split by direction for split networks

How to read it.

  • Where is the biology? Cell types with many DEGs and many enriched terms are where the comparison has the clearest effect.
  • Direction imbalance. A cell type whose DEGs are almost all one colour responds mostly in one direction. Consider running ORA with split_direction = TRUE for it, so the minority direction isn’t drowned out.
  • Many DEGs but few terms. The DEGs may be biologically scattered, may be poorly annotated in GO, or the universe may be too narrow. Check the run_go_ora() QC table.
  • Few DEGs but many terms. A small set of genes falls into many related GO terms (often one large family, such as ribosomal or histone genes). Check the driver-gene plot before trusting those terms.
  • Terms but no network clusters. The terms don’t share enough genes to connect at the current overlap threshold (see section 2).

Caveats.

  • DEG counts depend strongly on cells per group. A cell type with 2,000 cells will find more DEGs than one with 50, even for the same effect size. Don’t compare raw counts across cell types as if they measured effect strength.
  • The number of network clusters depends on the resolution. More clusters is not “more biology”.

2. Overlap threshold diagnostic

plot_overlap_threshold(net_result)

What it shows. Two panels.

Top: histogram of pairwise Jaccard overlaps. For every pair of enriched terms that share at least one DE gene, the Jaccard overlap is shared genes / total distinct genes. The dashed line is the overlap_threshold used to build the network: pairs at or above it become edges. The subtitle reports how many of all term pairs share any gene.

Bottom: what each threshold would keep. Across a range of thresholds:

  • Kept (green): terms with at least one edge.
  • Dropped (isolates) (orange): terms with no edge. These are removed from the network entirely: they don’t appear in the network plots, go_term_df, driver genes, or wordclouds.
  • Edges (right panel): number of connections.

How to read it.

  • The threshold should sit before the orange line rises. If many terms are dropped at your threshold, you are discarding enriched biology. Lower the threshold, or accept that those terms are unrelated to the rest.
  • Watch the edge count. Too low a threshold connects almost everything into one hairball, and Leiden then has little structure to work with. Too high a threshold leaves a few disconnected fragments.
  • A good threshold keeps nearly all terms while cutting the edges well below their maximum. In the histogram it usually falls just above the large mass of very small overlaps (pairs sharing one gene out of many).
  • Steps in the curves are normal. With small gene sets, Jaccard values take a limited set of values (1/5, 1/4, 1/3, …), so the histogram has gaps and the curves move in jumps.

Typical values. 0.1 to 0.3 for most data sets. The default is 0.1.

What to change. overlap_threshold in run_comparison_networks().

3. Leiden resolution sweep

plot_leiden_sweep(net_result)

What it shows. The network is re-clustered at each resolution, with 10 different seeds at each. Three panels share the x axis (resolution). The dashed line marks the resolution the network was built with.

Panel Meaning Line / band
Clusters Number of Leiden clusters Mean / range across seeds
Modularity How well separated the clusters are: the share of edge weight inside clusters, compared with what random wiring would give. Always measured at resolution 1, so values are comparable across the x axis. Mean / range
Stability (ARI) Agreement between the partitions from different seeds (adjusted Rand index; 1 = identical) Mean / range across all seed pairs

How to read it. Look for a plateau: a stretch of resolutions where

  • the cluster count is flat,
  • modularity is high and roughly flat, and
  • stability is close to 1 with a narrow band.

A resolution inside such a plateau gives clusters that reflect real structure in the network rather than the particular seed or the exact resolution you chose. If the dashed line sits on a steep part of the cluster-count curve, small changes in resolution would change your clusters: move it onto a plateau.

Interpreting the panels together.

  • Rising cluster count, falling modularity. Clusters are being split past the network’s natural structure. Go lower.
  • Stability dips with a wide band. At that resolution, different seeds give different clusters: the partition is ambiguous. Avoid those resolutions.
  • Stability of 1 at the extremes is not meaningful on its own. At very low resolution everything merges into one or a few clusters, and at very high resolution clusters approach single terms. Both are perfectly reproducible but uninformative. Always read stability together with the cluster count and modularity.
  • Modularity peak. The resolution with the highest modularity is a reasonable default if there is no clear plateau.

Modularity values. Above about 0.3 suggests meaningful community structure; GO overlap networks are often 0.5 to 0.8, because related terms form tight groups.

What to change. leiden_resolution in run_comparison_networks().

Notes.

  • The default objective is modularity, where resolutions around 1 are standard (the default is 1). With objective_function = "CPM", resolution means something different (an edge-density cutoff) and needs much smaller values, such as 0.01 to 0.1. Pass resolutions = seq(0.005, 0.1, by = 0.005) to the sweep in that case.
  • Clustering is seeded (seed = 1234), so rerunning gives the same clusters. The sweep varies the seed deliberately, to test how much the result would change without that fixed seed.
  • Networks with very few nodes can’t be swept meaningfully; the wrapper skips them with a message.

4. Driver genes per cluster

plot_driver_genes(net_result, de_df)

What it shows. For each Leiden cluster (columns), the top_n DE genes (rows) that appear in the most of that cluster’s GO terms.

  • Dot size is the share of the cluster’s terms that contain the gene. 100% means the gene is in every term of the cluster.
  • Dot colour is the gene’s log2 fold change (red = up in the numerator, blue = up in the denominator). Grey if no de_df was supplied.

How to read it.

  • Name the module from its genes, not only its terms. GO term names are generic (“regulation of cellular process”); the driver genes say what is actually changing.
  • Large dots for one or two genes mean the cluster exists because a few genes are annotated to many terms. The cluster may represent one gene’s annotation breadth rather than a coordinated program. Treat it with care.
  • Many medium dots mean the cluster is supported by a broad set of genes shared across its terms: a more convincing module.
  • Mixed colours within a cluster mean its genes move in both directions. This matches a grey (mixed) node colour in the network plot and is common for regulatory programs.
  • The same gene driving several clusters (it appears in more than one column) links those modules. They may be one program that Leiden split; try a lower resolution.
  • Watch for housekeeping families. Ribosomal (Rpl/Rps), mitochondrial (mt-), and histone genes can dominate clusters through sheer annotation volume, and can reflect technical differences between samples.

Rows are ordered by the first cluster each gene drives, so the plot reads roughly along a diagonal.

What to change. top_n for more or fewer genes per cluster.

5. The network plots

Each network gets three plots with the same layout ($plots in each network result, also saved as PNGs).

Plot Node fill Use it to
plain Direction: red = up in numerator, blue = up in denominator, grey = mixed See which regions of the network are up or down
leiden Leiden cluster (legend on the left) See the modules; match them to the driver-gene plot and wordclouds
zscore Continuous direction z-score, blue to white to red See how strongly each term leans one way

In plain and leiden, node shape also shows direction (circle = up, square = down, diamond = mixed). In all three, edge width shows Jaccard overlap and node size shows the number of DE genes in the term.

The direction z-score. For each term, z = (n_up - n_down) / sqrt(n_up + n_down), using the term’s DE genes. It combines how consistently the genes move with how many genes support it:

  • A term with 9 up and 1 down genes: z = 2.5 (clearly up).
  • A term with 3 up and 2 down: z = 0.45 (mixed).
  • A term with a single up gene: z = 1.0 (up, but weakly supported).

Terms are called up or down when |z| is at least zscore_threshold (default 1) and mixed otherwise. Raise it (for example to 2) for stricter direction calls.

The output tables also keep the mean and median log2 fold change for each term. The mean can be pulled in the opposite direction by one gene with an extreme fold change; the median and z-score are more robust.

With split_direction = TRUE every term in the _up network is up and every term in the _down network is down, so the plain and zscore plots are a single colour. Use the leiden plot and driver genes for those networks.

Quick reference

Symptom Likely cause Try
Many terms dropped as isolates Overlap threshold too high Lower overlap_threshold
One giant hairball cluster Threshold too low, or resolution too low Raise overlap_threshold, or raise leiden_resolution
Dozens of tiny clusters Resolution too high Lower leiden_resolution (check the sweep)
Clusters change between runs with different seeds Resolution in an unstable region Move the resolution onto a stability plateau
A cluster driven by one gene Annotation breadth of that gene Interpret with care; check its terms
Driver genes are ribosomal or mitochondrial Housekeeping or technical signal Check QC; consider whether the module is biological
Many DEGs, few terms Scattered biology, or a narrow universe Check the ORA QC table; try use_tested_universe both ways
Most terms are mixed Up and down genes share annotations Run ORA with split_direction = TRUE
Terms enriched, but no network No two terms overlap at the threshold Lower overlap_threshold
